articles.title: Physics-Consistent Generative Hologram Design for Multifocal Femtosecond Laser Fabrication
articles.authors: Bowen Chen, Hao Wu, Xiaoxu Rao, Wenji Yang, Zeye Li, Jincheng Ni, Jiawen Li, Dong Qing Wu, Yanlei Hu, Chaowei Wang
institutions: University of Science and Technology of China
articles.summary: Multifocal phase holograms let one femtosecond pulse expose many voxels at once, but weighted Gerchberg–Saxton (GSW) retrieval must iterate for every new target and does not optimise exposure quality directly. PhyFlow is an invertible flow network that maps a target focal pattern to a phase-only hologram in a single inverse pass, trained with differentiable Fourier-optics losses on diffraction efficiency, focal uniformity and shape fidelity. Across focal counts and array sizes it matches or beats GSW on energy concentration and focal balance while cutting generation time per hologram by 98.8%. Written arrays show more uniform dot areas, narrower line-width spread and fewer stray features.
articles.why: Hologram generation fast enough to change per layer or per scan line removes a main bottleneck of SLM-based parallel femtosecond writing.

articles.title: Uncovering the thermolysis conversion mechanisms of 3D nanoprinted silica glass
articles.authors: Jiajie Liang, Lisa Hoffmann, Paul Albrecht, Jens Bauer
articles.summary: Printing a hybrid preform by 2PP and converting it with heat is the main route to 3D-printed glass, ceramic and metal microstructures, yet the conversion is poorly understood. Starting from a POSS-based resist, the authors follow the transformation into silica glass with correlated thermal, mechanical and spectroscopic measurements, linking microstructure to shrinkage, colour and mechanics. Depending on the end point, parts range from rubber-like to ceramic-hard, with tensile strength up to 6 GPa.
articles.why: A process map for turning 2PP prints into silica glass, needed for printed micro-optics that must survive heat and high laser power.

articles.summary: Femtosecond-laser-induced selective etching (FLISE) is mature in fused silica but had not been shown in glasses that transmit into the mid-infrared. This first demonstration uses a gallate glass transparent to about 6 µm. HCl was the most effective etchant: with 100 kHz, 0.7–0.85 µJ pulses and perpendicular polarization, etch rates exceeded 4000 µm/h with aspect ratios up to about 15 in 1 M HCl. Thermal modelling and annealing indicate a narrow window below roughly 300–350 °C and point to oxygen-related defects behind the selectivity.
articles.why: Opens 3D channels, couplers and optofluidic parts in a glass that works out to 6 µm, where fused silica stops.

articles.authors: Jake L. R. Smith, Renae N. Gannon, Calina A. Glynn, James H. Naismith, Jorge Filevich, Michael Grange
articles.summary: Cutting electron-transparent lamellae out of thick (>100 µm) high-pressure-frozen tissue is the bottleneck for in situ cryo-electron tomography. Cryogenic femtosecond pulsed laser ablation (cryo-fs-PLA), targeted by cryo-fluorescence, removes bulk material from mouse brain tissue before serial cryo-lift-out. The authors set ablation parameters and rates for two wavelengths, and tilt series from lamellae near ablated sites remain largely vitreous. articles.authors: Guglielmo Troyer, Pourya Heidari Orojloo, Ali Gökhan Demir
articles.journal: Journal of Physics D: Applied Physics
articles.summary: Lithium metal sticks to punch dies and blades, so solid-state battery anodes need non-contact cutting. Remote femtosecond cutting of free-standing lithium foil was tested with two spot sizes in pulsed and burst modes. With the small spot, burst mode raised the cutting speed from 1.0 to 7.0 m/s; with the larger spot both modes reached 4.0 m/s. A two-temperature model reproduces the burst gain at fixed average power, and instability at small spots is traced to molten lithium closing the kerf.
articles.why: Metre-per-second speeds make ultrafast lasers a realistic production tool for lithium-metal anodes.

articles.authors: Yitong Chen, Li Nan, Zhijie Han, Yuxuan Li, Qingwei Zhang, Zihui Dong, Yuming Sun, Zhe Lin, Gangyi Zhu, Shanglu Yang
institutions: Nanjing University of Posts and Telecommunications
Shanghai Institute of Optics and Fine Mechanics, CAS
articles.summary: In ultrafast glass welding, Kerr self-focusing can pull the interaction zone away from the geometric focus and off the interface. Fused-silica welds were made with pulse durations from 262 fs to 10 ps while ICCD imaging tracked the plasma emission. Each duration puts the emission at a different depth within the first 2000 pulses, and the position keeps drifting as pulses accumulate, changing weld shape, location and shear strength. A ray-optics model that includes the Kerr effect reproduces the trend.
articles.why: Explains why weld position moves with pulse duration and gives a simple model for keeping the melt pool on the interface.

articles.authors: Niladri Ganguly, David Grojo, Pol Sopeña
articles.summary: Writing inside silicon with infrared ultrashort pulses is hampered by nonlinear propagation that clamps the energy density at the focus. The authors use the polarization-dependent diffraction efficiency of a liquid-crystal SLM to split one beam into two coaxial foci, with axial spacing and intensity balance set by the encoded quadratic phase and the input polarization. Reflection from the silicon back surface makes the two pulses meet head-on behind a single lens. Probing the excitation dynamics shows near-critical plasma densities that conventional focusing cannot reach.
articles.why: In-volume modification of silicon has long resisted femtosecond writing; a one-lens counter-propagating geometry is a simple way to push the deposited energy density higher.

articles.authors: Ruolan Luo, Yanting Fu, Jiale Qiu, Junshan He, Jinhao Zhou, Bingfeng Fan
articles.summary: Clean Bessel-beam dicing of sapphire relies on cracks linking continuously along the cut line. The pulse-energy threshold for that was mapped for pulse widths from 640 fs to 9.8 ps at several pulse spacings. The threshold first falls and then rises, with its minimum near 1.6 ps: shorter pulses lose energy to plasma shielding, while longer ones melt and diffuse heat, relaxing the residual stress that drives the crack.
articles.why: A concrete pulse-width setting, around 1.6 ps, for lower-energy sapphire dicing on LED and cover-glass lines.

articles.summary: Tomographic volumetric additive manufacturing (TVAM) cures millimetre-to-centimetre parts in seconds at tens-of-micrometre resolution, while 2PP reaches sub-micrometre detail only over sub-millimetre fields. This printer runs both on one platform with one resin: TVAM first builds a millimetre-scale body on a glass rod, then 2PP adds fine features inside or on its surface, with no resin change or intermediate post-processing. The TVAM pre-polymerised volume also eases the following 2PP step. Printed parts span three orders of magnitude in scale and carry 830 nm details.
articles.why: Puts sub-micrometre resolution only where a part needs it, the practical route to millimetre-scale micro-optics and scaffolds without days of 2PP writing.
